claim: Traffic signal phases adapt through a local feedback mechanism similar to myxomycete conduit thickening, where each intersection independently adjusts green time based on queue length measurements.
mechanism: Each intersection continuously monitors queue length and adjusts green time proportionally to the measured queue, creating a positive feedback loop where longer queues receive more green time. This mimics the thickening of conduits in response to higher flow rates in slime molds.
evidence: Slime molds optimize conduit thickness based on flow rates
Local traffic measurements can inform signal timing decisions
Distributed systems can achieve global optimization
assumptions: Queue length is the primary determinant of optimal green time
Intersections can operate independently without coordination
The system will naturally converge to an optimal state
expected_failure_modes: Inability to adapt to network-wide traffic patterns
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis introduces a biologically-inspired local adaptation mechanism that doesn't require central coordination, unlike traditional traffic signal optimization systems.
testability: The hypothesis can be tested by implementing a system where each intersection adjusts green time based solely on its own queue measurements and measuring network performance.
falsifier: If implementing local queue-based green time adjustment leads to persistent oscillations in signal timing or increased network-wide congestion compared to fixed timing plans, the hypothesis would be falsified.
